comments.author: @mxguy2438
comments.text: In the human world, intelligence is largely derived from focused early training. Musical "savants" are typical examples of this. We are all working from similar hardware... so if you want to be a savant, you will give up greatly in many other areas as this most effective early training window focuses in a narrow area. You simply will not be a great generalist if you are a savant in a single area. So efficiency comes from giving up useful things in one area to get really good at another area. In the context of AI, the cost of a large model is tied to the number of connections it makes with the data. A single AI trained from larger dataset will ultimately be more intelligent across all areas, but the optimized cost would be astronomical. Smaller models can be nearly as good in focused areas for pennies relative to the cost of larger ones due to fewer connections between data points. A large group of small models can be nearly as good across most areas for a fraction of the cost of a single large model... basically applying a different set of model weights based to fit the query. This tech will continue to progress with the brute force training technique combined by the down-selection of training data that we use now, but not be able to fully mature until the widespread application of quantum computing, where the model weights and probably the training dataset itself will be determined at inference, effectively providing a custom trained model for each and every context/query. When we look at a problem as a human, and another human comes and looks at a problem and comes up with a different answer, we would say these answers come from different perspectives. I suggest we start using "perspective" in the world of AI specialists as different specialists will approach a given problem differently.

The continuing advances are interesting, if not slightly mind-blowing, and, to that end, somewhere deep within my #QuantumWarmWetAndWild brain, I think embodiment is part of the definition of AGI. Without embodiment, it's a cheap shot to call anything AGI. We want to see: not just a cool servo-bot, not just an impressive program on a hard drive, not even the combination of the two. An AGI would be out here enjoying the sun, learning to ride a bicycle, scratching an itch for no traceable reason, and being capable of reproducing via atoms and molecules in an environment-dependent way with a counterpart AGI if it's consentual among them, etc. etc. etc. I'm not great at describing it, but, embodiment matters, and it's a long ways away.
That 85% threshold for a computer program to achieve, seems like a good benchmark for the moment, but to call that achievement AGI is sort of wishful thinking, like declaring winners in a game that's still underway and nowhere near finished.

comments.author: @DGPT10
comments.text:
The "efficiency" metric for the sake of an AGI argument is nonsense.
There are a lot of dimwitted folks who are inefficient, but nonetheless perfectly "generally intelligent" by the standard of reasonable doubt. 

Further, "cost" in terms of dollars is simply a measure of value and totally arbitrary since there are factors like "how much energy prices happen to be today". Imagine a model "solves" this ARC2 test with the exception of it "costing" $1 per task. Now, you take that model and put it on a hydro farm with cheap electricity and now it has a cost of $0.10 per task. Now it's somehow more intelligent because it cost less to perform the task? Give me a break.

I'm all for a test that incorporates efficiency and having that as a standard and a requirement to earn a prize. You're just not testing intelligence at that point. If the measure were "flops" or "energy consumption" while the hardware is constant, I can get behind that. For example, two models running on the same hardware, they both succeed at the task but one is either (1) faster or (2) consumes less energy, and arrives at the same correct solution, yes, that can be interpreted as increased intelligence. But "general" intelligence should not have arbitrary goal-post metrics attached to it.
